issues.subject: Inside Gemini: How Google Runs Product for Its Model

headlines: Google's Gemini PM Tulsee Doshi shares how product management works for frontier AI models, blending consumer taste, enterprise rigor, and research partnership in ways traditional playbooks don't cover.

The scarce skill in AI product is specifying exactly what 'good' looks like through precise evals (benchmark tests with clear win/loss definitions), not just reading benchmarks—a capability finance and operations hires can develop as well as engineers.

Successful AI product teams prototype features that don't yet work (60% working, 20% mediocre, 20% reach) so they move first when model capabilities catch up, rather than shipping perfect products too simple for tomorrow.

Every model release is a zero-to-one reset; Gemini ships on conviction about key signals (basic evals, real user behavior, glimmers of light) rather than green-lighting 100 teams, because no checklist predicts novel capability.
Model personality matters as much as benchmark scores—the best PMs actively use every model themselves to understand how it actually works with users, not just trusting numbers.

sections.title: How Product Managers Weigh Customer Requests Against Unpublished Research
points: Gemini's three customer types (Google products, internal teams, external API developers) submit conflicting requests, but requirements alone produce boring models.

The critical imbalance: customers don't see where researchers are investing and can't request features they don't know are possible, so product managers must have an established seat with research teams to learn where breakthroughs are happening.

This partnership requires calibrating to each researcher's motivation—some want synthesis of customer needs, others want help scaling their vision—and building trust so PMs can shape research direction earlier in the process.
One capability (like Deep Research) can serve three customer types, making platform-level consolidation essential rather than stacking individual feature requests.

sections.title: The Core Skill: Defining Good Evals Through 20 Replicable Examples
points: An eval is a benchmark test with clear definitions of what constitutes a win and a loss; the scarce skill is choosing which evals matter and specifying them precisely enough for researchers to optimize toward.

Start with 20 prompts exemplifying the problem, replicable and unambiguous—this forces vague asks like 'improve information architecture' into concrete specifications that align teams and seed sustainable eval development.
Best-in-class evals take weeks to build; Tulsee describes this as 'the skill we're still building and learning too,' meaning it's learnable but underestimated.

'Technical' on the model team means thoroughness—digging 2 levels below a 95% benchmark score rather than accepting numbers at face value—and this skill is more about rigor than computer science background, making it learnable from finance, consulting, or operations backgrounds.

sections.title: Prototyping the 60-20-20 Feature Mix: Ship Today While Betting on Tomorrow
points: Teams prototype features the current model can't fully handle yet (the 'glimmers of light' where small improvements unlock major value) while shipping what today's model does well, rather than trying to build a perfect product for present capabilities.

When the next model releases weekly, having features in testing means being first-to-market; if you over-engineer for today, you anchor on products too simple for tomorrow's capabilities, and if you build features completely unsupported, you ship broken products.

The target mix: 60% working well, 20% mediocre performance, 20% reach (ambitious but possible)—this ensures feedback loop specificity drives research direction upstream without shipping broken features.
This approach flips the traditional risk calculus: the risk isn't building on uncertain ground, it's over-optimizing the present and missing the capability curve.

sections.title: Shipping Models on Conviction, Not Checklists: The Zero-to-One Release Pattern
points: Google's traditional launch machine (hundreds of teams green-lighting a release) cannot work for models because each release is a fundamentally new product nobody has used yet, so shipping requires conviction about which signals matter most.

The signal hierarchy: run basic evals first, then put real users on the model ASAP, then ask only two questions—is anything fundamentally broken, and are there glimmers of light in behavior (longer conversations, harder tasks, repeat usage)?
User behavior is the tell—models worth shipping show measurable changes in how users interact (longer sessions, more complex queries, higher return rate), not just benchmark score improvements.

This cycle of shipping fast and reacting to each new model produces 'organized chaos,' and part of Tulsee's role is preventing that pace from burning out the team while maintaining strategic thinking.

sections.title: The Four Transferable Practices for PMs Anywhere
points: Build and prototype first to surface edge cases and validate the product is real before committing to research or requirements—40% prototype speeds learning more than perfect specifications.
Use all available models yourself (yours and competitors') because scores don't capture what models are actually like to work with, and that's what shapes user adoption and product personality.
Keep 20-prompt eval examples for any capability you're trying to evaluate, creating a replicable way to compare frontier models objectively and identify exactly where they fall short.
Hold a standing set of prompts to track how each new model 'feels' to use—simple asks like jokes, complex agentic tasks—so you develop taste ahead of data rather than chasing benchmark numbers.

sections.title: Building Model Personality Into Product: Why 'Vibes' Are Product Territory
points: Hundreds of benchmark numbers arrive with each model checkpoint, but none describe what the model is like to talk to; the failure mode is treating scores as the definition of the product rather than capturing personality.

The PM for NotebookLM (Simon Tokumine) is cited as owning vibes well because he actively uses every model, not just internal ones, and his observations about what he loves or questions inform product strategy.
A standing set of prompts—jokes, agentic tasks, edge cases—run against each checkpoint and against competitors reveals personality shifts that benchmarks miss and drives what users actually react to.
This is consumer PM skill (taste ahead of data) pointed at a product (the model itself) whose personality changes with every release.

sections.title: Establishing the PM Seat in a Research Organization
points: Researchers aren't accustomed to having product managers in their work, and the role has no standard definition, so successful PMs must understand what motivates each researcher and deliver against that motivation.

Some researchers want synthesis of customer needs; others have a strong point of view and want help taking their vision 'from point A to point B'—calibrating to the person determines whether the door opens for earlier opinion in the process.

Trust and delivery unlock influence; PMs who help researchers hit their goals earn increasingly early visibility into where research is heading, which becomes the basis for weighing customer requests.
The seat itself has to be established through demonstrated value, not organizational chart authority.
